newsitem.title: UK: Challenging times seen for UK oilseed industry.
newsitem.headline: Challenging times seen for UK oilseed industry.

text.p: UK oilseed producers face challenging times over the next five years as world demand for oilseeds outstrips supply, Martin Farrow, managing director of United Oilseeds, told a conference in Peterborough this week.
Farmers will have to adjust to more volatile prices and strange new plant varieties, he said.

"In the next five years we will see change, volatility and opportunity. Varieties and oilseed types will change out of all recognition. Volatility will increase as demand continues to increase ahead of production," Farrow said.
"The result will be considerable opportunity for UK oilseed producers provided they take up the opportunities presented to them," he added.

Global output of oils and fats has soared from 75.6 million tonnes to 96 million in just eight years. This was the result of both increasing population and rising affluence sparking per capita demand to rise.

"Despite advancing technology, we are losing the battle to meet the rising per capita demand for oilseeds. In 1987 one hectare of world oilseed production supplied 32.44 people, By 1996 this had fallen to 30.37 people a hectare," Farrow said.
Soaring demand has been met, in part, by increased planting.
Between 1987 and 1995 world planting of oil crops had risen by 27.4 million hectares -- equivalent to the whole U.S. soybean crop.

Plant breeding has not contributed significant yield increases in recent years. But that is changing. The arrival of new hybrids and genetically modified varieties will lead to a rapid increase in yield levels, he said.
World stocks of oilseeds, however, have been run down so that there is only 37 days supply available -- a post-war low.

The result is increased market volatility which has reached the stage where the gap between the peaks and troughs of prices makes the difference between high profits and significant losses for UK farmers.

"At the political level, the next round of World Trade talks needs to remove the Blair House agreement restricting European Union (EU) oilseed production. This (agreement) is now totally unnecessary," Farrow said.
On the marketing front farmers have to realise that all intervention protection has gone and they are now operating in a complex world market.
